newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Nizhny Novgorod mulls 5-year bond for '97.
newsitem.headline: Russian Nizhny Novgorod mulls 5-year bond for '97.

text.p: Russia's reform-minded Nizhny Novgorod region is likely to issue a five-year straight Eurobond in the first half of 1997, a senior official said on Tuesday.

"Most likely it will be a five-year paper similar to the sovereign one, but there is still no final decision," Stanislav Rybushkin, chief executive of the Regional Agency for Aid to Investment, told Reuters.
Straight Eurobonds have fixed interest rates, as opposed to rates set by the market.
Russia issued its first, $1.0 billion five-year Eurobond last November and government officials have said there will be another issue later this year.
Nizhny Novgorod already has an agreement with Moody's and Standard & Poors agencies to compile investment ratings for the issue, but contracts had not yet been signed, Rybushkin said.
Last week ING Barings of the Netherlands won a tender to lead-manage the Nizhny Novogorod issue. ING Barings invited MC-BBL bank as a co-leader.
Nizhny Novgorod's administration is in talks with Russia's KB Bank Yevrofinans to appoint a financial consultant for the issue.
Nizhny Novgorod governor Boris Nemtsov said last week that the issue's targeted volume was $100 million and mentioned June 1997 as the placement time.
Rybushkin confirmed the information, and said the major obstacle to the issue was an undeveloped legal base and tax laws.
The City of St Petersburg postponed its planned Eurobond because of a planned 15 percent tax on government securities.
It is still unclear whether profits from government securities will be taxed at a flat rate of 15 percent or at the usual profit tax rates of 35 and 43 percent.
But Rybushkin was not discouraged. "It was clear from the very beginning that there were no intructions and we together with the Finance Ministry must work on it," he said.
He said that the administrations of some Russian regions had discussed compiling a draft document on registering and taxing Eurobonds.
Besides Nizhny Novgorod and St Petersburg, Moscow and Sverdlovsk region are working on Eurobond issues.
Government officials said the state plan to coordinate Eurobond issues by regions and companies for fear of oversupplying the market.
But Rybushkin said he was sure there was demand for more Russian Eurobonds.
"The capacity of the market is so big there is space for everyone," he said.
